claims.text: Standard SPS fabrication of W–Cu composites leaves residual porosity and imperfect W–Cu interfacial contact.
Post-sintering laser treatment can selectively remelt the Cu matrix at W–Cu interfaces.
Microsecond-scale laser pulses producing approximately 1100–1150 °C at the interface will melt Cu without affecting the W structure.
An inert argon atmosphere will prevent oxidation during laser remelting.
In situ pyrometry or high-speed thermal imaging can ensure uniform laser-energy delivery and prevent overheating of W.
Short-duration high-temperature processing can rapidly produce and cool a molten metallic state.
Capillary forces will drive selectively molten Cu into interstitial regions, voids, and surface irregularities around W particles.
Capillary reflow of molten Cu will eliminate microvoids at W–Cu interfaces.
Rapid resolidification of the infiltrated Cu will create a continuous, defect-free metallurgical W–Cu interface.
Improved W–Cu interfacial contact will enhance thermal conductivity.
Improved W–Cu interfacial bonding will enhance mechanical properties and durability.
Laser-treated W–Cu will have significantly lower void content than untreated SPS W–Cu.
Laser-treated W–Cu will have greater thermal conductivity than untreated SPS W–Cu.
Laser-treated W–Cu will have superior mechanical durability under irradiation typical of fusion-reactor joints.
Restricting treatment to surface or near-interface remelting within approximately 1100–1150 °C will avoid thermal-stress damage and phase transformations in W.
Uniform laser processing of complex geometries may induce unwanted thermal stress or Cu-matrix microstructural changes.

Failure to obtain a statistically significant void reduction together with improvements in thermal conductivity and mechanical strength relative to untreated SPS controls would falsify the hypothesis.
